text.p: Lithuanian newspapers carried the following reports in their Monday editions. Reuters has not verified these stories and does not vouch for their accuracy:

- The functions of the newly-founded Ministry of European Affairs are expected to be approved during a meeting of the cabinet but officials at the foreign ministry fear they might be stripped of some key roles.

- People have been gathering at the Lithuanian parliament, TV tower and television headquarters to commemorate the sixth anniversary of the January 13, 1991 Soviet hardline coup. The newspaper writes about the victims of that night who survived the severe injuries of Soviet tanks.

- Foreign investment in Lithuania in 1996 could be estimated at more than $100 million, or $450 million since 1990, which is $121 per capita, says the head of the investment agency, Algis Avizhienis. The biggest investor is Motorola with $40 million and Philip Morris with $38 million followed by Statoil at $25 million.
- The new head of the tax inspection, Nijole Pitreniene, said in an interview that changes in the country's tax administration are inevitable.
- Latvian Prime minister Andris Shkele paid an unofficial visit to Vilnius on Friday but avoided talks on the most problematic topic -- the disputed sea border.

- An IMF mission will arrive in Lithuania on January 20 and will continue to work until February 4. It is expected that the memorandum which has been signed will be revised and a new letter of intention signed.

- The only participant in the international tender to manage the first free economic zone in Lithuania in Siauliai in northern Lithuania was Baltijos skrydis (Baltic flight) with three million litas share capital. It is 60 percent owned by the Baltic Fund (Rockefeller, Lazard Freres Asset Management and the Saudi royal family).
